teaser.text: Vylor Inc. sells the genetics, seed and feed-preservation products that help farmers grow crops and keep harvested forage usable. A dollar comes in when a farmer, retailer or licensee pays for that technology, and it goes out on research, production and delivery before the cycle turns into cash.

stock.title: Vylor stock forecast
stock.meta_description: Vylor stock forecast: weighted scenarios, operating drivers, real cash generation and what investors pay today.
stock.opening: Vylor's weighted price is $50.32 in October 2027, below today's price. It hinges on seed performance, net royalty growth, launches and cash conversion.
stock.closing: The full memo also explains Vylor's business, rivals, management and risks.

blocks.heading: Where could Vylor's shares be by 2029?

paragraphs.text: The probability-weighted forecast puts Vylor below today’s $72.18 in all three years. The weighted price is $50.32 in October 2027, a 30% loss including dividends. It rises to $56.53 in October 2028, a 21% loss. By October 2029, it reaches $63.88, still a 10% loss.
The range reflects execution risk. The bear case reaches $20.91 by 2029, while the bull case reaches $118.17. The forecast assigns 30% to bear, 52% to base and 18% to bull.

blocks.heading: What has to go right for Vylor, and what could go wrong?

paragraphs.text: The bear case gives $1,304M in 2027 and $1,166M in 2029. It assumes revenue still grows, but margins fall from 12.3% to 10.5% because seed volume, royalty conversion, launches and stand-alone costs disappoint. The bull case gives $2,017M in 2027 and $2,460M in 2029. It requires stronger adoption, retained royalties and successful launches. Price/mix contributed 3% and volume contributed 2% in 2025, supporting the possibility of growth, but corn still represented 71% of revenue and seed volume fell 3% in the June 2026 quarter.

blocks.heading: How much cash does Vylor really make?

paragraphs.text: Operating cash flow was $2,506 million in 2025. After capital spending, free cash flow was $2,160 million. After stock pay, which gives employees an ownership claim even though it uses no current cash, “real” free cash flow was $2,117 million.

blocks.heading: What does an investor pay for Vylor today?

paragraphs.text: At $72.18, shareholders value Vylor at $48,165.93 million. Its 4.5% free cash flow yield means about $4.50 of annual cash generation for each $100 invested. Free cash flow is operating cash left after capital expenditure. The reciprocal is about 22.2 times annual free cash flow, while the 4.4% real free cash flow yield offers a thinner cushion after subtracting stock pay.

earnings.title: Vylor earnings: guidance and what to watch
earnings.meta_description: Vylor expects results on November 11, 2026; management guides to $10,400 million of sales and $2,800 million of operating EBITDA for 2026.
earnings.opening: Vylor’s next results are expected on November 11, 2026. Watch progress toward year-end collections.
earnings.closing: The full memo answers how Vylor’s business works, who Vylor competes with, how Vylor’s management operates, and what risks Vylor faces.

paragraphs.text: For 2026, management guides to $10,400 million of sales and $2,800 million of operating EBITDA. R&D is targeted at 10.0% of sales in 2026–2027. By 2029, the sales target is $11.2–$11.9 billion. The operating EBITDA target is $3.3–$3.7 billion. Vylor expects $5.5–$6.5 billion of cumulative free cash flow from 2027–2029.

blocks.heading: How have Vylor’s revenue and profit changed?

paragraphs.text: Net income moved in the opposite direction, falling from $1,155 million to $1,022 million. The quarter included $78 million of separation expense, of which $64 million was after tax. Tax adjustments also supported earnings by $35 million, against $4 million a year earlier. Operations therefore improved more than the reported bottom line suggests, but the quarter still does not show broad demand acceleration.

blocks.heading: What should Vylor watch in the next results?

paragraphs.text: The November 11 results and November 12 webcast should clarify the standalone accounts, remaining separation costs and progress toward year-end collections. December brings a further test: whether workforce restructuring is substantially complete and whether recurring savings appear alongside declining implementation bills.
